claims.text: The stability of multi-metal nanoparticles across 473–1923 K is governed predominantly by the balance of mixing enthalpy and entropy.
Nanoparticles with near-zero or minimally nonzero mixing enthalpy maintain a kinetically trapped homogeneous solid solution.
Significantly positive mixing enthalpy promotes phase separation or elemental segregation at high temperature.
Significantly negative mixing enthalpy promotes phase separation or elemental segregation at high temperature.
The initial nanoparticles contain at least five metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and form a homogeneous solid solution.
Atomic-level mixing energetics mediate the competition between segregation-driving thermodynamics and kinetic barriers that preserve a metastable solid solution.
At elevated temperature, near-zero mixing enthalpy allows high configurational entropy to overcome the driving force for phase segregation.
Large deviations of mixing enthalpy from zero produce local fluctuations in atomic interactions.
These local interaction fluctuations nucleate segregated phases or elemental surface enrichment.
Segregated phases or elemental surface enrichment compromise structural and chemical stability.
Nanoparticles with near-zero computed mixing enthalpy will remain structurally and chemically homogeneous throughout 473–1923 K.
Nanoparticles with more positive or more negative mixing enthalpy will develop secondary phases or chemical inhomogeneity during heating.
The proposed relationship primarily applies when oxidation and other environmental reactions are minimized.
Kinetic effects or surface energies can cause deviations from predictions based on bulk mixing thermodynamics.

contradictions.description: The proposed stable state is described as kinetically trapped and supported by kinetic barriers, but the stated test conditions call for near-equilibrium behavior with limited kinetic barriers. These regimes are not equivalent and could yield different stability outcomes.
